definition: payroll_tax: annual household employee-side payroll tax: employee Social Security tax, employee Medicare tax, Additional Medicare Tax, and mandatory employee state payroll taxes. Exclude employer payroll taxes, FUTA, employer unemployment-insurance taxes, and self-employment tax (policybench/benchmark_specs.json)
engine: policyengine-us 2.15.17: employee_state_payroll_tax adds one <st>_employee_state_payroll_tax per state, and each adds the program contributions listed under engine_variables
test: Who owes the contribution under the statute. mandatory_employee_withholding: the statute puts the contribution on the worker and requires the employer to withhold it. optional_employer_pass_through: the statute makes the premium the employer's, and lets the employer deduct up to a share from wages without requiring it, so the employee amount runs from zero to the cap at the employer's choice.
method: One researcher per program read the statute, rules and agency pages and the engine source (2026-10-05). Two independent reviewers per program, one reading the statute and one the rules and agency guidance, then tried to refute each classification; review records each verdict. verification/law_research.json holds every record, quote, URL and verdict.

programs.employee_share_rule_text: Minnesota Paid Leave premiums "accrue and become payable by each employer" (Minn. Stat. 268B.14, subd. 1); the employer must pay at least 50 percent (small employers: at least a quarter of the full rate, subd. 5a), and employees pay through wage deductions only "the remaining portion, if any, of the premium not paid by the employer" (subd. 3), so the employee share runs from 0 to 0.44% of wages at the employer's choice.
programs.rate_2026: 0.88% total (0.66% for small employers); employee share at most 0.44% of wages up to the Social Security base

programs.employee_share_rule_text: Colorado FAMLI premiums are remitted by the employer (C.R.S. 8-13.3-507(2)), which "may deduct up to 50 percent of the premium" from wages (507(5)); an employer that deducts less is considered to have elected to pay the rest (7 CCR 1107-1 s. 1.4(6)(A)).
programs.rate_2026: 0.88% total; employee share at most 0.44% of wages up to the Social Security base

programs.program: Massachusetts Paid Family and Medical Leave
programs.employee_share_rule_text: Massachusetts PFML contributions are remitted by the employer (M.G.L. c. 175M, s. 6(a)), which may deduct up to 100 percent of the family and 40 percent of the medical contribution from wages (s. 6(c)) and may choose to deduct less (458 CMR 2.05(5)(c)).
programs.rate_2026: 0.88% total (0.18% family, 0.70% medical); employee share at most 0.46% of wages up to the Social Security base. Acts 2026 c. 101 (approved 2026-06-12) s. 25 strikes "40" in lines 22, 33 and 39 of s. 6 and s. 26 strikes "100" in lines 25, 33 and 43; s. 6 holds each figure exactly three times, in 6(c), 6(d) and 6(e), so the swap reaches the deduction caps (40% family, 100% medical). Its s. 45 applies ss. 25-26 "for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026"; its s. 43(a) asks for guidance on "the impact for employers and employees in calendar year 2027"; the DFML rates page captured 2026-06-17, after approval, still showed 0.46%, and DFML later (after the freeze) dated the change 2027-01-01. Under the literal s. 45 reading the 2026 cap would be 0.772% ($1,351.02 for scenario_081).

programs.program: New York Paid Family Leave and Disability Benefits
programs.law_citation: N.Y. Workers' Compensation Law ss. 209(3)-(4) and 210(1)
programs.employee_share_rule_text: New York's covered employer must provide disability and Paid Family Leave coverage; it pays the disability cost beyond what it collects (N.Y. Workers' Compensation Law s. 210(1)), no employer is required to fund Paid Family Leave (s. 209(3)(b)), and the employer "is authorized to collect" employee contributions up to the statutory caps by payroll deduction (s. 209(4)). The Workers' Compensation Board says an employer "is allowed, but not required" to collect them.
programs.rate_2026: PFL 0.432% of wages, at most $411.91; DBL 0.5% of wages, at most $0.60 a week ($31.20 over 52 weeks; a weekly payroll with 53 paydays in 2026 could reach $31.80)

programs.employee_share_rule_text: Each Connecticut employee "shall contribute" a percentage of subject earnings (Conn. Gen. Stat. 31-49g(b)(1)), and each employer "shall deduct and withhold" it (31-49g(b)(3)); there is no employer share.
programs.rate_2026: 0.5% of wages up to the Social Security base

programs.law_citation: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code ss. 984(a)(1), 986(a) and 2901
programs.employee_share_rule_text: Each California worker "shall pay worker contributions" (Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code s. 984(a)(1)), and each employer must withhold them in trust (s. 986(a)(1)); an employer that pays them for the worker still owes the worker's contribution, and the payment counts as wages (s. 986(a)(2)).
Each Pennsylvania employee "shall pay contributions" on all wages (UC Law s. 301.4(a)), and each employer "shall withhold, in trust" them (s. 301.4(b)).

programs.program: New Jersey TDI and FLI worker contributions
programs.employee_share_rule_text: Each New Jersey worker "shall contribute" to the TDI and FLI accounts (N.J.S.A. 43:21-7(d)(1)(G)), and each employer "shall ... withhold in trust" the contributions (43:21-7(d)(1)(E)).
programs.rate_2026: TDI 0.19% and FLI 0.23% of wages up to $171,100
programs.note: scenario_008's payroll output is already excluded (r05_nj_worker_ui: the engine omits the NJ worker UI and workforce contributions).

programs_without_a_benchmark_household.note: No benchmark household with wages lives in these states (two Washington households, scenario_002 and scenario_111, have no wages), so no reference depends on them. Each was researched once (verification/law_research.json, key OTHER) and not adversarially reviewed; payroll_mandatory_scope.py does not touch them.
